Question 1 · draft, Andrew to confirm

What has cell division already influenced, and what can we still change before harvest?

Start with the variety and the stage of this block.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 3–5 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 16–17, 35–3604 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm

The stage changes the decision

  • Cell division contributes to fruit size potential.
  • Later growth increasingly involves cells expanding; processes can overlap.
  • Use crop load, canopy and water observations to judge what may still be influenced.
What a test would show

Leaf or sap analysis reports sampled Nutrient status. It does not measure fruit cell number or predict final size.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 3–5 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 16–17, 35–36, 4405 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm
02
Question 2 · draft, Andrew to confirm

Size, firmness, Brix: where is my block most likely to fall short?

What is the fruit outcome you want, and what evidence have you got?

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 4, 6–8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, p. 4406 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm

Work back from the fruit outcome

  • Compare crop load and fruit growth with the outcome you want.
  • Check whether canopy condition and water supply may be limiting the crop.
  • Where evidence supports a Nutrient need, build the prescription blend around that need.
What a test would show

Soil and leaf or sap results add Nutrient evidence. Read them with crop observations and pack-out records; they cannot explain pack-out on their own.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 4, 6–8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 44, 4907 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm
03
Question 3 · draft, Andrew to confirm

Calcium in the leaf isn’t Calcium in the cherry. How do I know it is reaching the fruit?

Be clear about what was sampled before interpreting the result.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry shuck-fall article, 2026 · Development Guide, pp. 5–608 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm

A leaf result is not a fruit result

  • Calcium has a role in cell-wall structure.
  • Interpret the sample alongside fruit development, water conditions and canopy growth.
  • A leaf result alone cannot establish fruit Calcium or predict firmness.
What a test would show

Leaf, sap or paired-leaf DSA results describe the sampled leaves. They do not directly measure Calcium delivery into fruit.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, p. 23 · Development Guide, pp. 5–6 · Cherry shuck-fall article, 202609 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm
04
Question 4 · draft, Andrew to confirm

What can one leaf test tell me, and what can’t it?

Which result would actually change the decision?

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 10, 12–15 · Development Guide, p. 610 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm

Choose the test for the question

  • Start with the decision you need to make.
  • Keep the sampling method, leaf age, date and crop stage with the result.
  • Compare like with like, then check the result against the block.
What a test would show

Soil, leaf and sap tests measure different material. DSA compares separately sampled leaf ages; it does not directly measure root activity or reserves.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 10, 12–15 · Development Guide, pp. 6–711 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm
05
Question 5 · draft, Andrew to confirm

What should I be setting up for post-harvest while the bins are still filling?

The last pick is not the end of the tree’s season.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, p. 8 · Andrew Smith, The Hidden Season, pp. 18, 2812 / 16
Draft, Andrew to confirm

Plan for the canopy after picking

  • A functional canopy can continue contributing to reserves after harvest.
  • Review water supply and Nutrient evidence while the canopy remains active.
  • Match post-harvest decisions to the block without unnecessarily encouraging late growth.
What a test would show

Soil and plant analysis can inform rebalancing. A leaf or sap result is not a direct measurement of the tree’s carbohydrate reserves.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, p. 8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 30, 33, 44 · The Hidden Season, pp. 18, 2813 / 16

All ten original question options

Draft, Andrew to confirm. Source: Hybrid-Ag webinar question draft, 30 September 2026. Premises about timing, Nutrient “take-over”, cracking and testing remain subject to the current claim gates.

  1. Cell division is closing. What has it already decided, and what is still up for grabs before harvest?
  2. Size, firmness, Brix: which one is my block most likely to fall short on?
  3. What should I be setting up for post-harvest while the bins are still filling?
  4. Calcium in the leaf isn’t Calcium in the cherry. How do I know it is reaching the fruit?
  5. When does Potassium take over from Calcium, and how do I stop one crowding out the other?
  6. Soil, foliar or fertigation: from here to harvest, where does each one earn its place?
  7. Rain close to harvest: what can nutrition do about cracking, and what can’t it?
  8. One leaf test tells the story. Does it?
  9. My soil test says balanced. Why does the tree still run short when demand peaks?
  10. The canopy is carrying the crop now. How do I tell whether the leaves are keeping up?

Changes from the earlier draft

1. Current orchard evidence replaces a blanket assumption that cell division is closing.

2. Crop load, canopy and water decisions come before any Nutrient response; testing limits are explicit.

3. The questions follow the guide through fruit outcomes to post-harvest, with the final five still awaiting Andrew’s choice.

Slide 1 · 1:00

Where is your crop now?

Draft words for Andrew to adapt: “I’m Andrew. I grow cherries at Smith’s Fruit in Taminick and lead the Hybrid-Ag horticulture team. Tonight I want to look at where your crop is now, what you want from it, and what you can still influence.”

Ask the guide’s opening question: “If you had to describe your crop in 30 seconds today, what would you say?” Give growers time to think before moving on.

[check C01] Nathan and Andrew confirm date, start time, time zone and total session length. This deck allocates about 25 minutes to prepared material; open discussion is additional.

[check C02, C11] This is a review draft, not approved presentation copy. Andrew confirms the final five questions and wording; Nathan takes the finished deck to Amos before external use.

P01: the cover now uses Andrew’s portrait from his existing The Hidden Season presentation (file dated 29 March 2026), page 2. This is historical reference photography, not a claim about today’s crop. Confirm permission for this webinar; the original capture date and orchard location are not established.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Grower Webinar Development Guide, pp. 1–2

Slide 2 · 3:00

Where are your blocks now?

Use Andrew’s guide to compare early, mid and late varieties. Ask whether the season is early, late or close to normal locally, then invite other districts to describe their own position.

[check C03] Replace every blank with observations collected near the webinar: representative varieties, phenological stage, crop-load assessment, fruit diameter or growth, canopy observations and expected harvest. Do not infer this from the proposed October date.

Ask: “Do you actually know your crop load, or do you just know that you’ve got a good crop?” Keep it conversational. A crop-load count and an impression are different sorts of evidence.

P02a, P02b, P02c: three real, dated orchard photographs showing the selected maturity groups. These are a single comparison visual, not three claimed current states.

The guide proposes 3–4 minutes for a seasonal snapshot. Keep this to three minutes here so there is room for the five discussion threads.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 3–4

Slide 3 · 0:30

Five questions for tonight

Provisional selection from the ten-question bank: Q1, Q2, Q4, Q8 and Q3, in that order. All ten original options remain in the review panel and printable notes. None is represented as Andrew’s approved final selection.

Andrew’s guide changes the treatment: establish stage and crop load first, diagnose before discussing an intervention, work back from the desired fruit outcome and finish with next season.

The overview is a five-question index, not five technical points to teach at once. Each question gets its own slide and answer visual.

Hybrid-Ag · Webinar question drafts, 30 September 2026 · Development Guide, pp. 3–8

Slide 4 · 0:30

What has cell division already influenced, and what can we still change before harvest?

Adapted from Pinecone draft Q1. Removed “cell division is closing”, because the guide distinguishes varieties and blocks rather than assuming one stage for everyone.

Ask growers which variety they have in mind. Let someone describe the block before talking through the physiology.

Use the guide’s prompt: “Has your management changed as the physiology of the tree has changed?” Do not assume what growers have been applying.

[check C04] Andrew to confirm the final question and the simplified growth diagram on the next slide.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 3–5 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 16–17, 35–36

Slide 5 · 3:00

The stage changes the decision

Keep the physiology brief. The point is to change the question as the crop develops, not to prescribe a universal calendar.

[check C04] Andrew to review the diagram, including whether pit hardening and overlapping processes need showing for the chosen varieties. It intentionally contains no days, percentage gains or cultivar dates.

Ask which observation would change a decision this week: crop load, fruit growth, canopy condition or irrigation performance. Do not imply that an extra application can recover potential already lost.

Potassium may be relevant during fruit growth, but do not say it “takes over” from Calcium or give a universal Calcium:Potassium ratio. Any Nutrient interpretation depends on the result, method, stage and block context.

End at testing: a leaf or sap result adds Nutrient evidence. It cannot count fruit cells, directly measure photosynthesis or guarantee the eventual fruit size.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 3–5 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 16–17, 35–36, 44

Slide 6 · 0:30

Size, firmness, Brix: where is my block most likely to fall short?

Provisional draft Q2. The terms describe possible outcomes, not a claim that one treatment improves all of them.

Use Andrew’s guide: “What’s the biggest risk to achieving the fruit outcome you’re aiming for?” Give the grower time to answer.

Ask what they know about fruit number, current growth and water supply before narrowing the conversation to nutrition.

Brix is a soluble-solids reading from the fruit sampled. Do not present it as a measure of whole-tree carbohydrate reserves.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 4, 6–8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, p. 44

Slide 7 · 3:00

Work back from the fruit outcome

Keep the desired fruit outcome and its market context specific to the grower. Do not invent a size target, Brix target, pack-out percentage or expected response.

Use the guide’s question: “Of all the things you could do to your crop this week, which one would make the biggest difference, and why?” Ask for the evidence behind the choice.

Where a Nutrient need is supported, discuss a custom or prescription blend first. The application layers are Soil Primer, Foliar and Fertigation; suitability is an agronomic decision for the block. No standard product, rate or tank mix is recommended here.

[check C04, C05] Andrew to confirm any diagnosis, remaining management options and the test interpretation before adding a real example. Do not imply late crop-load changes or extra Potassium will reliably rescue size or pack-out.

P03: historical hands-and-cherries photograph from The Hidden Season, page 2. It illustrates the subject only and provides no evidence of crop load, measurements or a treatment result. Confirm reuse permission, or replace with an approved dated block photo and observations.

End at testing: soil and plant results can inform Nutrient decisions, alongside fruit and orchard measurements. Keep any previous season’s result clearly dated.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, pp. 4, 6–8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 44, 49

Slide 8 · 0:30

Calcium in the leaf isn’t Calcium in the cherry. How do I know it is reaching the fruit?

Provisional draft Q4. This is a question about the evidence, not a claim that a DSA directly measures fruit Calcium.

Ask what was sampled, when it was sampled and what decision the grower is trying to make.

[check C04] Andrew to confirm how much transport physiology is useful here. Avoid an unverified numerical threshold or a fixed application window.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry shuck-fall article, 2026 · Development Guide, pp. 5–6

Slide 9 · 3:00

A leaf result is not a fruit result

Keep the answer narrower than the original marketing tie-back. Comparing young and old leaves may add context; it is not proof of transport into the cherry.

[check C04] Andrew to confirm the practical sampling approach, limits and interpretation for this discussion. A suitable fruit measurement would need its own method and reference context.

No spray frequency, Calcium rate, fruit threshold, firmness or cracking outcome is implied. Calcium status is one part of the discussion, not a guarantee against weather or other causes of poor quality.

If asked about a product, first establish the crop requirement and evidence. This draft names no product and gives no composition, compatibility or application recommendation.

End at testing: be explicit about what a test actually sampled and what it cannot establish.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, p. 23 · Development Guide, pp. 5–6 · Cherry shuck-fall article, 2026

Slide 10 · 0:30

What can one leaf test tell me, and what can’t it?

Adapted from draft Q8, “One leaf test tells the story. Does it?” The wording invites a useful comparison rather than dismissing a valid test method.

Use the guide’s diagnostic question: “If you’re going to intervene in this crop tomorrow, what evidence tells you that intervention is actually required?”

Ask whether the question is about soil supply, sampled plant status, fruit growth or something else. A test is useful when it can improve that decision.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 10, 12–15 · Development Guide, p. 6

Slide 11 · 3:00

Choose the test for the question

Explain what each test reports without declaring a universal winner. Soil analysis is not a direct measure of actual root uptake; a leaf concentration is not the Nutrient content of the fruit.

For sap or DSA, use the laboratory’s sampling method. A comparison between young and old leaves does not directly measure movement rate, root activity or whole-tree carbohydrate reserves.

[check C04, C05] Andrew to select one consented, de-identified report example if useful. Retain laboratory, method, units, sample date/time, leaf age, crop stage and recent applications. Do not combine raw results across different methods as if directly comparable.

The diagram is a comparison of test scope, not a product-performance chart. No trial data or diagnostic thresholds have been invented.

End at testing: agree the question first, then choose the sample and decide how its result could change the next action.

Hybrid-Ag · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 10, 12–15 · Development Guide, pp. 6–7

Slide 12 · 0:30

What should I be setting up for post-harvest while the bins are still filling?

Provisional draft Q3. If the webinar is before picking, frame this as planning ahead rather than claiming that the audience is already harvesting.

Use Andrew’s closing prompt from the guide: “When the last cherry comes off the tree, is your season finished, or are you already managing next year’s crop?”

Link this season’s fruit to canopy condition, the post-harvest period and decisions for the following season. Do not promise a next-season result.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, p. 8 · Andrew Smith, The Hidden Season, pp. 18, 28

Slide 13 · 3:00

Plan for the canopy after picking

Use the existing post-harvest material for context, but do not repeat its older absolute percentages or fixed recovery windows.

[check C04] Andrew to confirm the stage-specific wording and what is realistic for the selected varieties, canopy condition and local weather.

P04: historical orchard image from The Hidden Season, page 11. Exact block, capture date and phenological stage are not established. Use as reference photography only; Andrew confirms suitability and permission or replaces it with a dated post-harvest example.

A prescription response should follow evidence of the block’s Nutrient needs. No guarantee of next year’s set, size, firmness or yield is made.

End at testing: agree which soil or plant sample would help the next decision and when it would be useful, using the appropriate method.

Hybrid-Ag · Development Guide, p. 8 · Cherry Nutrition Playbook, pp. 30, 33, 44 · The Hidden Season, pp. 18, 28

Slide 14 · 0:30 + open discussion

What are you seeing in your blocks?

[check C07] Andrew nominates two or three growers we work with and asks their permission ahead of time. Leave names blank until agreed; do not script a testimonial or manufacture a problem.

Invite those growers to open the discussion, then take registration questions and questions from the room.

For each thread, clarify the block and stage, listen to the problem and return to what a soil, leaf, sap or DSA test could show. If it cannot answer the question, say so.

Pause the planned-presentation timing for open discussion. [check C01] Nathan and Andrew confirm total session length and how to manage unanswered questions.

Hybrid-Ag · Webinar brief, 30 September 2026 · Development Guide, pp. 2, 6–7

Slide 15 · 2:00

Out of ten, how did the orchard pack out last season?

Ask the out-of-ten question exactly as written in the current brief. [check C08] Andrew should clarify that this is the grower’s assessment of the season, not a reported pack-out percentage.

Listen to the reason for the score before continuing. Ask what information would help make the next decision.

Only now reveal the closing offer, using the on-slide button, the right arrow or Space. The offer is never shown on an earlier slide or mentioned in earlier speaker notes.

Suggested close: “If your test results are spread across different labs or bits of paperwork, we can help bring them together and chart the trends. If that would be useful, let’s agree what you want included and the next step.”

[check C09] Nathan confirms scope, the grower’s go-ahead, who gathers the records and the follow-up process. Do not imply that cleaning up records by itself provides an agronomic diagnosis or guarantees an outcome.

Hybrid-Ag · Webinar brief and Playbook Lead Campaigns state, 30 September 2026

Slide 16 · 0:30

Thanks for the conversation

[check C10] Nathan confirms recording permission and the follow-up email before this statement is used externally. Add Andrew’s approved contact details or a confirmed reply route; do not invent an email or phone number.

Thank the growers for contributing their own observations. Say how unanswered questions will be followed up once that process is confirmed.

Retain the draft label until Andrew approves the content and wording and Nathan has run the finished deck past Amos [check C11].
